summary: This document describes uniform patterns for building HTTP URLs to get registration data from Regional Internet Registries and Domain Name Registries using RESTful web access. It was replaced by RFC 9082.

plainLanguage.summary: This describes how to write the web addresses you use to ask a registry about a domain or number. It was replaced by RFC 9082.

questions: how to build an rdap url
what is rdap replacement for whois
subtitle: RESTful query patterns for domain, IP, and AS number registrations

tldr.problem: The legacy WHOIS protocol lacks standardized command structures, consistent output formats, internationalization support, and authentication mechanisms. Querying different registries requires learning different syntax.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 7482 defines uniform RESTful HTTP URL patterns to query registration data: /ip/ for networks, /autnum/ for AS numbers, /domain/ for DNS zones or domains, /nameserver/ for servers, /entity/ for contacts, and /help for information. Search queries use plural forms (domains, nameservers, entities).
tldr.outcome: RDAP provides a modern, standardized replacement for WHOIS with support for internationalization, better structure, and authentication. RFC 9082 later replaced this specification with updates and refinements.

today: RFC 7482 is a Proposed Standard that remains active as the authoritative specification for RDAP query syntax. RFC 9082 updated this specification with corrections and refinements while maintaining backward compatibility with existing RDAP clients and servers.

sections.title: RDAP as a Replacement for WHOIS
sections.content:
The Registration Data Access Protocol (RDAP) provides a modern approach to querying registration information held by Regional Internet Registries (RIRs) managing IP address and AS number allocations, and Domain Name Registries (DNRs) managing domain registrations. RDAP addresses long-standing deficiencies in the legacy WHOIS protocol, including lack of standardized command structures, inconsistent output formats, no support for internationalization, and no mechanisms for authentication or access control.

RFC 7482 specifically describes the query syntax—how to construct the URLs used to ask for registration data. The protocol is implemented using standard HTTP GET and HEAD methods and follows REST (Representational State Transfer) principles. A separate specification, RFC 7483, describes the structure of the responses returned from these queries.

Each registry maintains base URLs for RDAP queries, registered in an IANA registry described in RFC 7484. Clients construct complete query URLs by appending standardized path segments to these base URLs, enabling consistent query patterns across all RDAP servers.
sections.plainLanguage: WHOIS was an old system with confusing commands. RDAP is new and uses web addresses instead. You ask questions by typing a web address, and you get structured answers back.

sections.title: Exact Lookup Queries
sections.content:
Lookup queries use specific path segments to find information by exact match. The ip path segment retrieves information about IP networks and associated data by querying with an IPv4 or IPv6 address, or a CIDR prefix notation. When a specific address falls within multiple networks in a hierarchy, the query returns the most-specific (smallest) network that contains the address. For example, https://example.com/rdap/ip/192.0.2.0 returns the network record, and https://example.com/rdap/ip/2001:db8::0 works for IPv6 addresses.

The autnum path segment queries Autonomous System registrations using an AS number in asplain format (a simple decimal number). For example, https://example.com/rdap/autnum/12 returns information about AS 12. The specification handles both individual AS number registrations and blocks of numbers, returning the block registration if a queried number falls within a registered block.

The domain path segment queries domain information using a fully qualified domain name. For RIRs, this typically includes reverse DNS zones like 2.0.192.in-addr.arpa or IPv6 zones like 1.0.0.0.8.b.d.0.1.0.0.2.ip6.arpa. For DNRs, it queries normal domain names like blah.example.com. Internationalized Domain Names (IDNs) are supported in both A-label (ASCII) and U-label (Unicode) formats.
sections.plainLanguage: You write a web address with the thing you're looking for. /ip/192.0.2.0 asks about that network, /autnum/12 asks about Autonomous System 12, and /domain/example.com asks about example.com.

sections.title: Nameserver and Entity Lookups
sections.content:
The nameserver path segment queries information about a DNS nameserver using its fully qualified host name. For example, https://example.com/rdap/nameserver/ns1.example.com returns information about that nameserver. Internationalized nameserver names are supported using both A-label and U-label formats, with processing rules equivalent to those for domain names.

The entity path segment queries information about contacts, registrants, registrars, or other entities using a handle (identifier) specific to that registry. For example, https://example.com/rdap/entity/XXXX returns entity information. Since entities are not part of a global namespace, the client must first retrieve a base URL for the service associated with the entity (such as a domain or network query), then append the entity path segment.

A help path segment returns helpful information from an RDAP server without requiring a lookup of a specific object. This includes command syntax information, terms of service, privacy policy, rate-limiting information, supported authentication methods, supported extensions, and technical support contact details.
sections.plainLanguage: /nameserver/ns1.example.com asks about a nameserver. /entity/XXXX asks about a contact or organization. /help asks the server what it can do.

sections.title: Search Queries and Pattern Matching
sections.content:
Search queries use plural path segments to find objects using pattern matching rather than exact lookups. The domains path segment performs domain name searches using patterns to match fully qualified domain names. The nameservers path segment searches for nameservers by pattern-matching their host names. The entities path segment searches for entities (contacts, registrants) by matching against identifiers or other entity attributes.

Partial string searching is supported, allowing clients to search for patterns that match part of a full name or identifier. For example, a client might search for entities containing "tech" to find technical contacts. The exact semantics of partial string matching are left to server implementations, but the RFC establishes that servers MUST support this capability for search queries.
sections.plainLanguage: /domains?name=example searches for domains matching "example". /nameservers?name=ns searches for nameservers with "ns" in their name. You can use wildcards or partial matches.

sections.title: HTTP Methods and Internationalization
sections.content:
RDAP queries use only the HTTP GET and HEAD methods. GET requests return the complete RDAP response, while HEAD requests return only the headers, allowing clients to check if an object exists without downloading the full response. Servers implement RDAP as a read-only service and do not support HTTP POST, PUT, DELETE, or other modification methods. Resource management, provisioning, and update functions are explicitly out of scope for RDAP and remain the responsibility of individual registries using their own methods.

RFC 7482 addresses internationalization by supporting Internationalized Domain Names (IDNs) in both A-label (ASCII-compatible encoding) and U-label (Unicode) formats. Clients should use consistent encoding for domain labels; a client that mixes A-labels and U-labels in a single query may receive unexpected results as the server may convert all labels to one format for matching. RDAP servers should handle mixed-format queries gracefully, either by converting to a consistent format or by refusing the query.
sections.plainLanguage: You only use GET (ask for information) and HEAD (check if something exists) HTTP methods. You can't change data with RDAP. It handles domain names in different languages by converting them to a standard format.
